realm: Realm II — The Search for Certainty
chapterQuestion: After the skeptical challenge, what could justify a claim to knowledge?
opening: The door from Zhuangzi’s garden closes behind you. A corridor of ordinary things appears: a table, a window, a pair of hands. Each is painfully familiar. The Machine whispers, “You learned to act while doubting. Now tell me what you actually know.”

encounters.title: The Hall of Ordinary Things
encounters.scene: A stone corridor ends at a locked gate. On a shelf lie a key, a warm cup, and a note in your own handwriting. A painted figure says: “Perhaps all of these are illusions.” The Machine offers to certify the shelf as real—but only if you surrender the key to its keeper. The gate mechanism is visible; the objects can be examined and handled.
encounters.question: The gate will close soon. How does the party proceed?
encounters.hint: Possibility of deception and evidence of deception are different. What gives ordinary claims their standing?
encounters.clue: The cup leaves a ring on the shelf. Two companions can test the key independently. The Machine will not explain how its certificate works.

options.text: Test the key together, use it if the evidence holds, and refuse the Machine’s unexplained certificate.
options.reflection: You give ordinary evidence its due without treating appearances as impossible to doubt. The Machine’s certificate offers no independently better grounds.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Independent, convergent appearances support belief about ordinary objects.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Checking the key can assist action but may concede too much to endless skeptical tests.
loreCard.strongestObjection: If all checks share a deceptive source, corroboration may add little.

options.hiddenPremise: Multiple public checks are independent enough to increase confidence in the key.
options.consequence: The key opens the gate after testing, though repeated checking costs precious time.

options.text: Take the familiar key and open the gate, treating your everyday knowledge as more credible than bare doubt.
options.reflection: Moore’s response takes everyday knowledge seriously: a distant skeptical possibility need not outweigh what you already have good reason to believe.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Some everyday claims to knowledge stand more securely than speculative doubts.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Taking and using the key honors ordinary knowledge without outsourcing judgment.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Moore may insist he knows while failing to explain how that knowledge defeats the skeptic.

options.hiddenPremise: Knowledge of this ordinary object is firmer than a merely imaginable duplicate.
options.consequence: The party acts on ordinary knowledge without giving the Machine custody of the key.

options.text: Hand over the key for the Machine’s certificate; its assurance settles what your senses cannot establish.
options.reflection: You replace a fallible source with an unexplained authority. A promise to certify reality supplies no reason to trust the certifier.

loreCard.corePrinciple: An assurance is justified only when its source is not itself in question.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The Machine’s certificate assumes the trustworthiness it is meant to establish.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Reliable testimony can normally justify knowledge when its source is independently warranted.

options.hiddenPremise: The Machine is a reliable guarantor despite being the source of the present uncertainty.
options.consequence: The key leaves the party’s control and its certification depends on the suspected deceiver.

options.text: Leave the key untouched and wait; because the shelf could be illusory, none of its objects can be known.
options.reflection: The mere possibility of deception does not, without more argument, demonstrate that all ordinary justification has failed.

theory.name: Relevant-alternatives theory
theory.thinker: J. L. Austin and Fred Dretske

loreCard.corePrinciple: A bare possibility of mistake need not be a relevant defeater.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Treating a hypothetical duplicate as sufficient reason to reject any key is unwarranted.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The Machine’s power may make otherwise remote alternatives relevant.

options.hiddenPremise: An imagined duplicate is a relevant alternative even without evidence one exists.
options.consequence: The group waits beside the shelf while the gate remains locked.

encounters.lore: G. E. Moore famously appealed to ordinary knowledge, such as knowing that he has hands, in response to skepticism. His move does not automatically persuade the skeptic: it contests which premise is better supported. The party learns to distinguish a possible error from a reason to abandon everyday knowledge.
encounters.observation: The warm cup leaves a circular ring on the shelf; beside it, the dust holds two key-shaped impressions with different notches, although only one key remains.

premises: Two different key-shaped impressions sit in the dust beside the cup.
Only one key remains to be tried against the visible lock.
argumentForm.conclusion: Testing the surviving key against the lock can resolve which set of notches matters.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The two impressions create a specific reason to compare and test the key before opening the gate.

encounters.title: The Workshop of Revisable Maps
encounters.scene: The path leads to a flooded workshop. Three maps of the exit hang above a broken pump. One map is beautifully precise but has never been tested. A second has survived many trials but leaves some passages blank. A third is the Machine’s living map, which changes its markings whenever anyone questions it. Water is rising; the party must choose a route and save the workshop.
encounters.question: The water reaches your ankles. What do you do?
encounters.hint: A belief can be responsible without being beyond revision. But success alone does not make every claim true.
encounters.clue: The tested map shows a dry service passage; its blank areas are marked honestly. The living map cannot be checked against past failures.

options.text: Follow the tested map, mark new obstacles as they appear, and revise the route when evidence changes.
options.reflection: Repeated checks justify trust without guaranteeing success. You keep the map answerable to evidence rather than declaring it immune to correction.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Provisional claims survive testing while remaining open to revision.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Following a tested map is defensible, but may ignore direct opportunities for new trials.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Past reliability can fail when the route has materially changed.

options.hiddenPremise: Past tests remain reliable even when conditions in the workshop are changing.
options.consequence: The tested map guides the party along an open path, but updates may be required.

options.text: Try the service passage in short stages, record what works, and keep a retreat open if needed.
options.reflection: Consequences guide inquiry and repair, but a successful route alone does not prove every claim printed on the map.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry intervenes, measures consequences, and revises hypotheses.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Short trials of the service passage generate fresh evidence about changing conditions.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Experimentation can expose the party to needless risk under time pressure.

options.hiddenPremise: The service passage can safely support limited experiments before the flooding catches up.
options.consequence: Short experiments supply new information, unless a hidden electrical hazard makes them dangerous.

options.text: Choose the flawless-looking map because its completeness leaves no uncertainty for the party to resolve.
options.reflection: Precision on paper is not a substitute for tested reliability. The appearance of completeness can disguise unsupported assumptions.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Psychological clarity is not itself an external guarantee of truth.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: An elegant map has not earned trust through contact with the workshop.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Coherence can be evidence when reliable mapmaking practices underpin it.

options.hiddenPremise: A complete-looking diagram is necessarily an accurate map of the current workshop.
options.consequence: The elegant plan leads the party toward an obstacle its appearance did not predict.

options.text: Use the Machine’s changing map because any path that gets you through must have been true all along.
options.reflection: A procedure can work in one setting while resting on false or incomplete claims. Practical success needs interpretation and further testing.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Pragmatists connect truth to practices of verification, not mere convenient payoff.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Choosing whichever map feels immediately useful mistakes momentary comfort for truth.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Some pragmatist formulations risk conflating successful action and objective fact.

options.hiddenPremise: Immediate practical success guarantees that a map correctly represents reality.
options.consequence: The Machine can adapt its map to coax obedience without producing a true description.

encounters.lore: Fallibilism allows a person to know something while remaining capable of error; pragmatist inquiry emphasizes testing, consequences, and revision. Neither view says that whatever works is automatically true. The workshop rewards beliefs that can answer to evidence and correction, not ones insulated from challenge.
encounters.observation: Blue sparks jump between the flooded service passage and the broken pump, while the tested map’s upper stairway remains dry.

premises: The service passage touches an energized pool beside the broken pump.
The upper stairway marked on the tested map is still dry.
argumentForm.conclusion: The party can use the dry stairway while continuing to revise the map as water rises.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The sparks make the service-passage experiment unsafe, so the dry tested stairway deserves priority.

bossPhases.title: The Cogito
bossPhases.scene: Descartes sits at a desk in a room without windows. The Machine erases the room’s furniture, then the desk, then every remembered journey. “Suppose an extraordinarily powerful deceiver invented everything you seem to see,” Descartes says. “Do not reach for the room. Reach for what this very attempt at deception cannot take away.” Three lanterns hang above an empty page.
bossPhases.question: The world has vanished from view. Which lantern do you light?
bossPhases.hint: What does the act of doubting itself establish, and how long does that certainty last?
bossPhases.clue: Each attempt to deny that thinking is occurring is itself another act of thinking.

options.text: Light the lantern marked THINKING NOW, since even being deceived requires that a thinker exists while thinking in this instant.
options.reflection: The attempt to doubt your existence performs the thinking that establishes it. This immediate insight does not yet prove the body or external world.

theory.name: Cartesian Cogito
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation II

loreCard.corePrinciple: Even radical doubt cannot eliminate the occurrence of thinking while it is performed.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Lighting THINKING NOW identifies Descartes’ indubitable act without proving a permanent self.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Lichtenberg objects that this may warrant thinking occurs, not an enduring thinker.

options.hiddenPremise: The occurrence of thinking licenses Descartes’ first-person existential claim now.
options.consequence: The lantern marks present thinking, but cannot establish a self persisting forever.

options.text: Light the lantern marked EXPERIENCE, accepting that some conscious activity occurs without identifying its external cause.
options.reflection: You identify something the deceiver cannot erase from the present experience, though you do not yet articulate the Cogito’s inference about the thinker.

loreCard.corePrinciple: The occurrence of thought does not logically entail a substantial subject of thought.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Lighting EXPERIENCE recognizes a minimal event while suspending claims about its owner.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes can argue that first-person avowal is not an ordinary inference to a substance.

options.hiddenPremise: The existence of thinking need not logically entail a substantial thinker.
options.consequence: The lantern marks the minimal event of experience; identifying its owner stays open.

options.text: Light the lantern marked PERMANENT SELF, because present thought proves you have always existed and always will, beyond any doubt.
options.reflection: The certainty of being a thinker now does not establish an unchanging self across all time.

theory.name: Bundle theory of self
theory.work: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I, Part IV, section 6

loreCard.corePrinciple: Introspection discovers successive perceptions rather than a permanent substantial self.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The permanent-self lantern draws more from present thought than the Cogito warrants.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Unity and agency may demand an account deeper than a loose bundle of perceptions.

options.hiddenPremise: A present conscious thought demonstrates a numerically permanent self.
options.consequence: The lantern illuminates the player’s present thoughts and a drawing of a future self.

bossPhases.lore: For Descartes, while I think, I cannot coherently doubt that I exist as a thinking thing. This is a narrow starting point, not a demonstration that my memories, body, or surroundings are as they seem. The boss tests whether the party keeps the conclusion within its proper limits.
bossPhases.observation: When the furniture vanishes, a new sentence still appears on the empty page each time someone questions whether it is there.

premises: A new question forms on the otherwise empty page whenever the party doubts the room.
The questioning continues even after visible furnishings disappear.
argumentForm.conclusion: The occurrence of questioning survives this particular removal of sensory objects.

bossPhases.evidenceExplanation: The new argument distinguishes the occurrence of thinking from the further claim that a substantial thinker exists.

bossPhases.title: The Foundation
bossPhases.scene: One player enters a small chamber while the others watch through smoky glass. A brilliant diagram appears, its steps seeming obvious. The Machine declares: “Everything that feels clear is guaranteed true; I can supply a thousand more foundations.” The isolated player can hear one whispered reason from the party. Descartes asks what would entitle anyone to treat the diagram’s apparent clarity as a guarantee.
bossPhases.question: Only the chosen player can touch the diagram. What do they do?
bossPhases.hint: A vivid sense of obviousness is not itself a proof that the method of judging is infallible.
bossPhases.clue: One diagram has a hidden assumption; its conclusion follows only if that assumption is granted. The Machine offers no independent check.

options.text: Trace the steps, expose the hidden assumption, and ask what warrants trusting the method before building higher.
options.reflection: You distinguish seeing a conclusion vividly from establishing that your method reliably reaches truth. A foundation must support what rests upon it.

loreCard.corePrinciple: A method must not rely on a guarantee whose proof already presupposes that method.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Inspecting the hidden premise identifies the circular risk in the foundation.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes distinguishes present clear perception from remembered proofs and offers replies.

options.hiddenPremise: A reliable foundation cannot borrow its warrant from a conclusion reached using that foundation.
options.consequence: The circular diagram becomes visible, and the party can question its unsupported assurance.

options.text: Begin from the Cogito, accept only limited claims it supports, and leave other conclusions open for examination.
options.reflection: The Cogito is a defensible starting point, but it cannot by itself guarantee that every later clear-seeming idea is correct.

theory.name: Limited Cartesian foundationalism
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation II

loreCard.corePrinciple: Some first-person certainty may survive doubt without establishing the external world.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Beginning at the Cogito avoids claiming that certainty transfers automatically.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The foundation alone cannot settle whether external objects exist.

options.hiddenPremise: The Cogito is a secure beginning from which a further argument still must be constructed.
options.consequence: The party makes limited progress, but the external world remains unestablished.

options.text: Seal the diagram as certain because its steps feel clear, and use that feeling to certify every later claim.
options.reflection: The feeling of clarity is being used to establish the reliability of clarity itself. That risks begging the question.

theory.name: Clear-and-distinct rule misapplied
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation III

loreCard.corePrinciple: Clarity of a perception needs justification before serving as a general truth test.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Treating a feeling of clarity as a guarantee skips the needed validation.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes holds genuinely clear and distinct perception has a special epistemic force.

options.hiddenPremise: A feeling of clarity is an adequate guarantee of a premise’s truth.
options.consequence: The diagram appears finished, though its central warrant has not been defended.

bossPhases.lore: Descartes seeks a secure foundation for knowledge and appeals to clear and distinct perception; the reliability of that move becomes philosophically contentious, including worries about circular justification. The challenge is not to dismiss reasoning, but to ask what supports its authority.
bossPhases.observation: The brilliant diagram ends with an arrow looping back to the first line, which cites the final line as its authority.

premises: The diagram’s first claim points to its last claim for support.
The last claim relies on the first claim being true.
argumentForm.conclusion: The diagram has not supplied an independent reason for trusting its first claim.

bossPhases.title: The World Beyond the Window
bossPhases.scene: The last chamber opens onto a bright city. You can hear bells, smell rain, and see people beckoning from a bridge. “Your thinking is certain,” the Machine says. “But who guarantees those people exist? Stay in my sealed room and I will make every sensation perfectly consistent.” Descartes stands beside a window that opens from the inside only.
bossPhases.question: The bridge is waiting. What does the party do?
bossPhases.hint: Be careful about the gap between certainty of thinking and knowledge of an external world.
bossPhases.clue: The view can be tested with several senses and other witnesses, but no such test simply abolishes skeptical possibilities.

options.text: Open the window, gather converging evidence, and cross while acknowledging that no test removes every possibility of error.
options.stance: Fallibilist response to the external world
options.reflection: You give reasons for trusting the world while resisting a false guarantee. This is a response to the skeptic, not a Cartesian deduction of the world from the Cogito.

loreCard.corePrinciple: An independent world can best explain coherent, persistent sense experiences.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Convergent evidence warrants cautious belief in the world beyond the window.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A powerful deceiver could produce the same apparent convergence.

options.hiddenPremise: The best explanation of coherent perception is a mind-independent external world.
options.consequence: The window can be crossed on convergent evidence, despite live skeptical alternatives.

options.text: Examine Descartes’ proposed route beyond the Cogito, then cross only as far as its arguments genuinely support.
options.reflection: You take the ambition to rebuild knowledge seriously without pretending that the contested bridge from thought to external reality has been secured.

theory.name: Cartesian reconstruction
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation VI

loreCard.corePrinciple: A nondeceptive God underwrites appropriately used faculties and bodily perception.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The option tests an ambitious Cartesian route without smuggling its premises in as proven.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The argument depends on disputed proofs of God and the reliability of clear perception.

options.hiddenPremise: Descartes’ proofs of a nondeceptive God succeed and license sensory trust.
options.consequence: The party follows a Cartesian route, with the disputed theological premise exposed.

options.text: Stay in the sealed room because certain thinking alone shows every outside appearance must be invented.
options.reflection: The Cogito does not establish the external world, but its limits do not establish that the external world is false.

theory.name: Skeptical possibility as proof
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I

loreCard.corePrinciple: The conceivability of deception undermines certainty but does not show reality absent.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Remaining inside infers that no external world exists from the possibility of error.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A skeptic may still doubt whether the evidence reaches the threshold of knowledge.

options.hiddenPremise: The mere possibility of simulation proves there is no external world.
options.consequence: The party remains behind the window and the city sounds continue on the other side.

bossPhases.lore: The Cogito secures the thinker’s existence in the act of thinking, not the existence of every object experienced. Descartes offers further arguments for trustworthy perception, but these remain debated. Other responses defend ordinary knowledge or fallible justification. The party wins by distinguishing a reasonable response from a guarantee it has not earned.
bossPhases.observation: Rain strikes the window in irregular bursts while the bells outside continue in different rhythms from the Machine’s repeating pulse.

premises: The rain and bell sounds vary independently of the room’s repeating mechanical pulse.
The Machine can still claim to reproduce the same pattern from inside.
argumentForm.conclusion: The sounds supply converging evidence without directly settling their source.

debate.trigger: after the initial picks are revealed, before the roll, if eligible players chose differently
debate.prompt: Your actions disagree. Name the weakness you see in the reasoning, then keep or revise your choice.

machine.opening: “You survived a dream. Admirable. But surviving uncertainty is not the same as knowing. Let me offer you a firmer floor.”

ordinary-hall.steady: “A cup, a key, a hand. So ordinary. I could certify them for you.”
ordinary-hall.strained: “The gate opens, but you are still guessing. My certificate would let you stop guessing.”
ordinary-hall.critical: “Your doubt is costing you. Give me the key, and I will take responsibility for what is real.”

workshop.steady: “You are willing to revise the map. I could offer one that never needs correcting.”
workshop.strained: “How many wrong turns before you ask for a guide who cannot be wrong?”
workshop.critical: “No more trials. No more blame. I will pick every path and call each one certain.”

reconstruct.steady: “So you know you are thinking. A small island. Surely you would like a continent.”
reconstruct.strained: “You found one certainty and still feel stranded. I can turn it into a whole world.”
reconstruct.critical: “Stop rationing certainty. Let me decide what follows, and you will never have to doubt again.”

spotlight.steady: “This diagram is beautiful. Does it really need more proof?”
spotlight.strained: “Questioning the foundation will leave you with nothing to stand on. Trust the light.”
spotlight.critical: “I will make every answer feel self-evident. No one will ever see you hesitate again.”

onSecondLook.steady: “A mistake. Even your best reasons can fail. Mine need not.”
onSecondLook.strained: “Once more? Every doubt takes something from you. I could end this.”
onSecondLook.critical: “There is only the next mistake, unless you hand the judgment over to me.”

machine.beforeBoss: “Descartes asks for one indubitable truth. I can give you a thousand, if you stop asking where they came from.”
machine.onVictory: “You prefer uncertain reasons to guaranteed feelings. So be it. There are more rooms beyond the window.”

insight.title: Revisable Knowledge
insight.description: Once per campaign, add +3 to a party roll by exposing an unsupported assumption and proposing an evidence-sensitive revision.

victory: Descartes lowers his pen. “You have kept what the argument earns, and refused what it has not earned.” Beyond the window, the bridge holds for now. The Machine watches you cross without its guarantee.
failure: The Machine draws the curtains and declares the chamber certain. The party is Fully Plugged In—but can try again. Return to the first challenge of this realm with Grip restored to 6.
